Chapter 1. Growing Up Between Two Worlds: Family, Identity, and Early Displacement
Childhood memories are such a curious mix, aren’t they? There’s warmth, laughter, and sometimes a deep confusion—especially if you’re growing up between two cultures. Picture a small apartment in postwar Japan, filled with the voices of both Japanese and Korean, and the quiet tension of two histories trying to coexist.
For this boy, whose mother was gentle and practical, and whose father carried the heavy pride of an outsider, home life was a balancing act. His mother did everything to keep their world together—while his father, restless and full of longing, struggled with being seen as a stranger in the only country his children had ever known.
At school, the reminders of being different were constant. Kids notice everything, don’t they? Sometimes it was a glance, sometimes a whispered comment, but always a message: you’re not quite one of us. The boy’s mother tried to shield him, but his father’s frustration only grew. All he wanted was a place where he could be respected, where his kids wouldn’t have to carry the weight of their heritage like a burden.
Life at home was simple, and money was always tight. No matter how hard the father worked, it never seemed enough. He’d talk about Korea as if it were a place of dignity and real opportunity—a land where they’d finally belong. The mother listened quietly, her worry showing on her face. She’d heard stories of life in the North, but sometimes hope is all you have when each day feels like a struggle.
Eventually, hope turned into a plan. North Korean propaganda made bold promises to ethnic Koreans living in Japan—jobs, equality, a better life. The father’s determination grew stronger with every passing day. The mother hesitated, caught between her husband’s dreams and her own fears. But the pressure kept building, and finally, the family decided to leave everything they knew behind.
The journey to North Korea was loaded with uncertainty. Imagine boarding a ship, saying goodbye to the only home you’ve ever known. The boy held tightly to his mother’s hand, old enough to sense the worry around him but too young to grasp just how much was at stake. All they really had was the promise of a new beginning—and each other.
When they arrived, they were welcomed with smiles and official fanfare. At first, it looked like the promises were coming true. They got a place to live and were celebrated as “returnees.” But it didn’t take long to see that things were different underneath. The language sounded familiar, but the rules were strict, and the father soon realized that respect wouldn’t come so easily. Now, the mother was the outsider, struggling to adapt in a world that felt foreign and unforgiving.
The children tried their best to fit in, but their Japanese background made them stand out. School was hard, making friends was even harder. The boy learned to stay quiet, to keep his head down. That “returnee” status—once a source of pride—quickly became a reason for suspicion. The father’s hopes for dignity faded with every new setback and harsh word.
As time went on, that sense of being out of place just grew deeper. The mother missed Japan—her family, tiny comforts, all the little things that made life feel familiar. The father’s frustration sometimes boiled over at home. The children watched, learning early that trust could be dangerous, and that hope was something fragile.
Still, these hard years planted the seeds of resilience. The family endured—not because life got easier, but because, well, what other choice did they have? The boy, shaped by loss and longing, began to realize that surviving meant letting go of old dreams and learning to live with uncertainty. What started as a hopeful journey was quickly turning into a test of endurance, and the toughest lessons were only just beginning.
